headline: Ethics watchdog chief steps back over historical sexual misconduct allegations
summary: Stuart Sterling, chief executive of the newly-formed Ethics and Integrity Commission (created by Labour to ensure probity in government), has stepped back from his role after allegations emerged from his time as a detective at Northamptonshire Police in the early 2000s. He was suspended in 2002 after being accused of inappropriate conduct with a female colleague, undergoing a disciplinary process that resulted in a sanction (reported as a two-week pay penalty—the maximum possible short of forced resignation at the time); police did not launch a criminal investigation. A second investigation into alleged misconduct in 2008 was also inconclusive, and Sterling denies it took place. He was subsequently promoted to detective sergeant and received commendations before leaving the force and joining the Cabinet Office in 2009, eventually becoming OBE. The government says it will "swiftly establish the facts" regarding the renewed allegations.

headline: Milburn's NEET review to propose major welfare overhaul with political risks for Labour
summary: Alan Milburn's long-awaited review of youth joblessness and NEET rates (Not in Education, Employment or Training) proposes sweeping reforms intended to rebalance welfare toward employment support. The review, due for publication, argues that young people under 25 should be blocked from sickness and disability benefits, and calls for a dramatic shift in spending: currently around £25 is spent on benefits for every £1 on employment support, and Milburn wants to move toward a 2-to-1 ratio instead. The underlying claim is that the NEET crisis costs the economy up to £125bn annually in lost output and welfare spending. The headline from Laura Kuenssberg notes this will be politically fraught for Work and Pensions Secretary Andy Burnham, as past attempts at welfare reform have triggered Labour rebellions. Milburn stresses this time differs because it proposes a permanent structural system rather than another passing scheme, and emphasizes employment, mental health support, and building a "good life" rather than just cutting benefits.

headline: Undercover documentary reveals welfare failures and possible unlawful placement at East Sussex asylum centre
summary: An ITV undercover documentary has exposed serious problems at Crowborough, a former military base in East Sussex used to house asylum seekers. The investigation, conducted by an undercover reporter posing as a welfare officer, found inadequate welfare checks and revealed that torture survivors may have been placed there unlawfully. The facility is run by a firm connected to billionaire asylum camp operator Graham King and is part of the government's broader strategy to end hotel accommodation for asylum seekers in favour of mass institutional sites. The documentary, "Inside The Asylum Camp," demonstrates that poor screening and inadequate oversight are having serious consequences for vulnerable residents.

headline: Welsh Labour leader admits party lost touch with voters ahead of post-election review
summary: Ken Skates, leader of Welsh Labour since his election to the role in July (after the party's historic May Senedd defeat), presented findings from an independent review at the Welsh Labour conference on 14 November. The review, conducted by Anand Menon, attributes Welsh Labour's collapse—the party fell to third place, losing two-thirds of its vote share and all but nine of its 60 seats, and incumbent First Minister Eluned Morgan lost her seat—to multiple failures: the party had stopped listening to voters, public services weren't improving quickly enough, and Labour had taken its support for granted. Skates acknowledged these "difficult" findings and vowed to rebuild trust and connection with the electorate. The party's loss in May 2026 was the first Senedd election defeat for Welsh Labour since the body's establishment in 1999.

headline: Government asylum detention plan criticised over proximity to sewage works
summary: The Home Office plan to build new secure detention facilities at Campsfield House immigration removal centre in Oxfordshire is facing objections over environmental conditions. According to a written submission from Thames Water, the proposed accommodation blocks would be situated just 20 metres from a sewage pumping station. Thames Water warned that detainees should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells from the facility. The plan is part of the government's broader strategy to expand detention capacity for asylum seekers.

headline: Government says it will consider raising age of consent following allegations against Russell Brand
summary: The government has indicated it will consider calls to raise the age of consent following allegations made public by Mia Latter, now 37, who waived her anonymity to claim she was orally raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 and he was 30. Brand is currently in jail. The Deputy Prime Minister stated that while changing the age of consent "would be a massive step," the proposal "deserves proper consideration and scrutiny." The case highlights a legal scenario—where an adult can lawfully engage in sexual activity with a 16-year-old—that campaigners and some survivors argue should be reconsidered.

headline: Opinion: Britain should veto UAE candidate for UN role over Sudan weapons allegations
summary: This is a Guardian opinion column by Steve Bloomfield arguing that Britain should use its veto power to block Lana Nusseibeh, a UAE-backed candidate, from a UN leadership position. The argument rests on documented UN investigations revealing that the UAE has supplied weapons and mercenaries to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a Sudanese paramilitary group accused of genocide in Sudan's ongoing war (which began in 2023). Bloomfield contends that Nusseibeh's role has involved "glossing the horror in Sudan" and that her appointment would be inconsistent with the UN's own investigative findings about Emirati involvement. The column notes that Nusseibeh appears to have backing from Russia and the US, but argues Britain has the power and responsibility to block her appointment.

headline: Modi's office summons Indian telecom secretary over use of fake court orders
summary: Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's office has summoned the telecom secretary following allegations that officials used fraudulent court orders. The details of the fake orders and their scope are not provided in the feed snippet available.

headline: Federal judge blocks Trump's Washington golf course redevelopment project
summary: A federal judge temporarily blocked Trump from proceeding with a redevelopment project at a Washington, D.C. public golf course, likely based on regulatory or procedural grounds, though specific details on the grounds for the injunction were not accessible.

headline: Appeals court rules federal government wrongly withheld highway funding from New York over immigrant licenses
summary: A federal appeals court determined that the U.S. government incorrectly withheld highway funds from New York in retaliation for the state's policy of issuing driver's licenses to immigrants, regardless of legal status. The ruling addresses a conflict between federal transportation funding conditions and state immigration policy implementation.

headline: Zelenskyy warns that US-proposed European security framework could undermine Ukraine by benefiting Putin
summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy expressed concern that a new European security framework being floated by the United States could inadvertently create advantages for Russia and Putin, reflecting ongoing tensions over how post-conflict security arrangements might affect Ukraine's strategic position and sovereignty.

headline: Incoming Democratic Congress unlikely to shift Trump's hardline Cuba policy despite skepticism
summary: Though a new Democratic-controlled Congress will view Trump administration's stringent Cuba policy with skepticism, political and parliamentary realities make near-term policy reversal unlikely; Cuba is expected to remain a low priority for Democratic legislators, and the administration shows no sign of softening its maximum pressure approach.
